b: i currently use obsidian for all my note taking and to edit the markdown articles that are rendered in this site. i have a paid subscription so that i can use sync to keep all my devices updated and be able to edit my vaults from anywhere but i don't think i use obsidian to its full potential yet. the ecosystem just seems to keep growing and growing. i have recently started using a couple of community plugins: smart typography and text snippets. i use the former to replace quotes to curly quotes and, perhaps more importantly, simple dashes to em dashes — i use em dashes probably a bit too much. i use text snippets to expand from a word to a frontmatter template i can easily fill out, instead of having to copy/paste from other articles. these have definitely made my life easier. as of 2025-02-20, obsidian is now free for commercial use.

p: The Pixelbook is an ultrabook launched in 2017 by Google, running ChromeOS. It had 6 years of software support and mine expired in June 2024. I have decided to wipe it and install Ubuntu on it around September 2023. Pasted image 20230921232931.png Photo by Google I've been a happy user of a Google P
b: the pixelbook is an ultrabook launched in 2017 by google, running chromeos. it had 6 years of software support and mine expired in june 2024. i have decided to wipe it and install ubuntu on it around september 2023. pasted image 20230921232931.png photo by google i've been a happy user of a google pixelbook for a few years. it has brilliant hardware and software. it's not a regular laptop, as it uses chromeos as an operating system. i would describe it as a computer for the mobile phone age: instantly on, simple, user friendly, very low maintenance and it just works. this might not be a big deal in 2023 but, in 2017, i can assure you it was. unfortunately, as for other main vendors, it also has finite software support from the vendor. every chromeos device has an expiration date, when it's no longer possible to install any updates. this wouldn't be necessarily a problem for 'regular' operating systems, where we can at least keep the apps up to date. in chromeos, the chrome browser is a central part of the operating system and can't be installed externally. this means, after the laptop expires, it will continue to function but it will not get the latest features and, more importantly, it will no longer receive the latest security patches, thus potentially exposing private data or be exposed to other attacks. it is possible to install android chrome from the google play store or install desktop linux chrome from the crostini container but none of these would provide a first-class experience and important integration with the rest of the operating system would be lost. interestingly, it is possible to have a lifetime of well supported chrome in a device using any other operating system but not on a google device, with a google operating system.

b: disclaimer: this article should now be obsolete. if you think the information is still valid and links to external urls have not rotted yet, do not follow this tutorial if you cannot afford losing your pixelbook. i accept no liability for any loss. posting questions in the subreddit r/chrultrabook is your best chance of getting expert help. introduction my google pixelbook expires on june 2024. i have decided i will not replace the hardware, so to replace chromeos, i have to reflash the bios, format partitions and install linux. i could do this next year but i actually missed using linux and gnome as my daily driver after years with chromeos and i3. i didn't expect an easy setup but i expected a stable experience once it was set up. this article describes how i've managed to install and use ubuntu on a google pixelbook as it's sole operating system. beware, it's not for the faint of heart. preparation besides thorough research, i personally didn't spend too much time preparing, possibly because chromeos is very oriented towards using the google services and the google drive, so most of the data was already located in the cloud. in any case, i would suggest backing up all your local data to the google drive. it should be a matter of dragging and dropping folders in the file manager. make sure you let the folders sync completely with the cloud otherwise, once the user data is erased, the data will be lost. secondly, we need to create a bootable usb stick with a linux distribution iso installer. i have chosen ubuntu desktop 22.04 lts for this case. i have used another linux machine to download the iso and burn it to the usb stick. once the iso was downloaded, i ran the command below to create the bootable usb stick: the device to use in the of field - /dev/sdb in my case - should be obvious by running lsblk in the terminal. i used an adapter between usb-a and usb-c to plug the usb stick to the pixelbook. there are many other ways of creating a bootable usb stick. in windows, rufus seems to be a popular choice. i've read reports selecting the 'dd image' mode is important later on. now, on to the hard stuff. developer mode despite of chromeos being linux under the bonnet, the google pixelbook is very well locked up and secure. it has proprietary bios, firmwares, etc. therefore, it's not possible by default to sideload an installer of an alternative operating system and install it side by side or in place of chromeos. one has to get access and reflash the rom with an open bios like coreboot to be able to do so. i have used the firmware utility script by mrchromebox described in his site to install the firmware. this script must be run in the crosh terminal. the terminal in the crostini container does not have full access to the hardware, so it's impossible to flash the rom from there. to get access to the crosh shell, the pixelbook must be in developer mode. one of the side effects of enabling the developer mode is essentially doing a factory reset to the pixelbook, so at this point you should be prepared to erase all local data. the developer mode is accessed via the recovery menu. to reboot to recovery, press and hold esc + refresh and then press the power button. once you see the recovery menu, you can let go of esc + refresh, as described here in step 3. to enable developer mode, press ctrl + d and confirm, as described here. the next time the pixelbook is started, it will show a welcome screen like it's being switched on for the first time. i believe the crosh terminal can be invoked from the first screen with a ctrl + alt + t. otherwise, you'll have to configure an account, login normally and finally invoke crosh using the same combination from there. removing write protection and flashing bios unfortunately, we can't just run the script and flash the rom, as the rom is write-protected at hardware-level. to disable the write protection, we have to simply disconnect the battery, a process that involves removing the back panel - where the battery is glued on - and disconnecting a flat cable from the motherboard, a process very well described in this ifixit article+replacement/103036). it's understandable if you don't feel confident proceeding with this madness. at this point, you can still boot to recovery, disable developer mode and restart normally to chromeos. there is another method described in mrchromebox's website that should be less invasive but requires a special debug usb cable, which i have not tried. assuming my readership was brave enough to go ahead with opening the pixelbook and disconnecting the battery, it is possible now to start the pixelbook, launch the crosh with ctrl + alt + t, type shell, launch the firmware utility script with as described in here, and select install/update uefi (full rom) firmware. this is the last time you'll see chromeos in this pixelbook, before shutting down. the battery can now be reconnected to the motherboard and the back panel reattached, to enable write-protection again. installing ubuntu and mitigating some quirks in the next reboot, you'll be greeted with the coreboot logo. chances are that you've rebooted with the usb stick plugged in but it is not being detected in the coreboot boot menu. the solution for me was to go back to the main/root menu, unplug the usb stick, wait a couple of seconds, plug it back again, wait ~3 seconds and check the boot menu again. it didn't work straight way with me and this could be quite distressing until it works. once you'll see an usb-related entry in the boot menu and select it, things will then become quite familiar if you've installed ubuntu before. in my case, during the whole installation process, the picture was flipped upside down. this shouldn't prevent completing the installation, if we ignore the awkwardness. in the first boot after the installation the picture was oriented correctly. by now, you should have everything working except, i think, sound and the top row of the keyboard. i have not tested whether input events from the stylus are being recognised but intend to do so soon. it would be great if the stylus still worked with it for some ad-hoc whiteboarding. to fix the sound and the keyboard, i have followed this thread in reddit. the important part entails installing the packages pixelbook-alsa and pixelbook-keybd from this folder in google drive. i have not tried the pixelbook-sensors package. sound and keyboard should now work out of the box. the only issue i have at the moment is, whenever i plug headphones in or out, the sound device is not switched automatically. it has to be done manually in the settings > sound dialogue, which is a bit a annoying. i'll try to fix this issue once ubuntu 23.10 comes out. other than that, it has been running quite stable so far, gnome is a very polished experience and, in the age of pwas and the cloud, i don't feel limited in any way. it would be great to have more than 8 gb of ram for more browser tabs.

b: - it’s march, the meteorological spring has started, the weather has been lovely in this part of the planet. after the snow bells, crocuses and daffodils are everywhere and cherry trees are blossoming. - there was formula 1 pre-season testing in bahrain and this week we have the first race of the season in melbourne. i have a lot to say about this but will spare my readership and just write a few commonplace ideas: the last season before major changes in regulation is usually the best with performance convergence across the field, where usually everyone asks themselves why are we changing the formula if this is so good?. on the other hand, mclaren seems to have made another step forward in performance — still to be confirmed — and this season could be a duel between norris and piastri, reminiscent of hamilton vs rosberg in 2014. - i’ve ordered a keychron k1 pro with pbt keycaps and brown switches. since i spend so much time typing, thought it would be nice to use something substantially better than the £20 mechanical keyboard i’ve been using in the past few years. it’s all about the small pleasures. - we used to slog almost 7 months straight after the christmas break and spend the first holiday period around the end of june but for the first time in 18 years we’ll be spending easter in lisbon, to better align with the school holidays. i think it’s great. - wish you all a fantastic week!

b: there’ll be more next week - see you then! ... and in the end, there was not more next week or anything else for over a year. to cut the story short, because this is not a 2025 review, life happened. 2025 was not a bad year, by any means, but it was a hard working year. normal parenting stuff---nothing out of the ordinary. years usually start optimistically and i was convinced a's sleeping patterns would improve like h's around the second year and we, the parents, would be less sleep deprived, but this time it was different. i have been planning (in my mind) a rewrite of the static site generator for most of 2025 and i finally decided to roll up my sleeves during the christmas break. the main new features are 1. incremental builds 2. using git to save checkpoints and derive created and modified dates, instead of relying on the os filesystem's ctime and mtime 3. generate rss feeds i had no idea what i was getting into with the incremental builds and how infinitely more complex the codebase has become. fast forward to last week, it felt most functionality was there and the most obvious bugs were fixed. it is still in beta but i'm doing a soft launch, not announcing for now in any of the usual channels. i think it's just a matter of updating and polishing some of the slash pages and it should ready for the general audience. i am hoping this will be a solid foundation of a slowly evolving platform. developing the static site generator has been fun but now it's time to turn my attention to actually using it---writing content.

b: - the site is still in beta. i haven't had the time to address what is still pending because... - last week was different because a. got hands, foot and mouth for the third time and had to stay at home recovering for two days, with my wife and i alternating with the nursing duties. because she had a blocked nose, a. did not sleep much due to the troubled breathing, so we ended the week exhausted. things are coming back to normal. - i finally seem to have solved a problem with the pixelbook that has been nagging me since i've started using linux on it. the variant with an intel core i5 cpu (the one i have) doesn't have a modern ssd; it has an emmc, which is basically an sd card soldered to the motherboard that can only do one operation at a time. this means the system is very limited in terms of i/o. when running i/o intensive tasks like e.g. upgrading the system, that completely saturates the system and even low level events like refreshing what is displayed on the screen or moving the mouse cursor around has to wait. this means that sometimes, especially when these processes would run unattended in the background, the laptop would freeze for minutes on end, rendering it completely unusable. the solution is mainly using a kernel scheduler that deprioritises this sort of tasks and reserves resource for anything essential. this way, even if these i/o heavy tasks may take longer to complete, you can ensure that your system will always be responsive. i may add something about this soon, in a page somewhere. - we've got to the end of the first quarter of the year, surely surprising many skeptics. it's time to look again at the yearly objectives and make sure things don't start to slide.

b: - it was the second week of easter holidays for h. and we decided to take the week off and spend it in the center parcs in the elveden forest, suffolk. - it is very much part of the family holidays industrial-complex and it is very formatted but we liked the format and would definitely go back again. two and five year olds are only able to enjoy about a tenth of what is on offer, so there is still lots of replayability potential. - h. definitely had a blast: "best holidays ever!". good, that's what we want to hear. - i was hoping to do loads of stuff and move the site from beta to something more stable and complete in the late evenings whilst staying there but the competition from reading the screwtape letters and watching the end of the season 3 of the chosen (mostly this), meant things are pretty much in the same state. no worries, we'll get there soon. - placed an order for a tricycle for our two year old a., who is a bit of a schumacher, and another helmet for h., one size up. - now, it's time to go back to the routine of work, school and nursery. my office day count is at zero in april so it's going to be an interesting rest of the month.

b: - the girls are asleep. i came online and thought about saying hi. - did i really write that i was going to have some interesting weeks ahead?? - besides the cosmological, has anything more mundane happened? let me see. - the joys of assembling flat-packed furniture, once again. we configured a tylko bookshelf on their website (#mytylko in the socials) and had it delivered all the way from poland. we're happy with the purchase; the living room looks a bit more civilised now. - h. had her first tooth fall out. it wasn't gory at all. - a's tricycle was delivered in the meantime. it was initially ignored, as her sister's scooter was still the centre of her life, but with some insistence, it seems to be her first choice now—much to my relief. - we're taking a break during the half-term and spending the week in portugal. a different airport and airline this time, and we've rented an airbnb for the first time. let's see how it goes.

p: - This was an important and busy week. The momentum was interrupted by this week's half-term break, but let's hope I can keep it going when I get back. - As I write this, we are in Estoril, the return flight is yet to happen and $N=1$, but flying to Lisbon with Ryanair from Stansted was quite straig
b: - this was an important and busy week. the momentum was interrupted by this week's half-term break, but let's hope i can keep it going when i get back. - as i write this, we are in estoril, the return flight is yet to happen and $n=1$, but flying to lisbon with ryanair from stansted was quite straightforward—with perhaps the exception of the shuttle transfer between the long stay car park and the terminal. in comparison to luton airport's, it had far longer queues, but it's a bigger airport and it's half-term. - yet again, i felt short changed by the car hire at the lisbon airport. - we've met with friends for an early dinner on sunday and it was lovely to catch up.

p: - It seems we've avoided some toasty days in the UK. The temperatures haven't been that different in Lisbon, but it's far more tolerable here. How come Estoril is 23 km from Lisbon but it's always 4 C colder? Is it the ocean breeze? - I could have spent my late evenings more unwisely than by reading
b: - it seems we've avoided some toasty days in the uk. the temperatures haven't been that different in lisbon, but it's far more tolerable here. how come estoril is 23 km from lisbon but it's always 4 c colder? is it the ocean breeze? - i could have spent my late evenings more unwisely than by reading the entire latest encyclical letter by pope leo xiv (via, e.g., simon willison). that is an understatement, of course; i thought the reflection about what sort of post-ai world we'd rather have and his view that when we apply ai (or any other technology), we should optimise for the dignity of the human person were very pertinent. - sorry, most people have ai coming out of their ears already but kyla scanlon's latest, long and well researched newsletter about ai and jobs was also an interesting read. - i have migrated to antigravity cli but noticed that it makes changes without showing the diff and seeking confirmation. it's true that otherwise it would be a clunky workflow and not very high-throughput, but are we being encouraged to just vibe code it? - the return flight from lisbon to stansted was perhaps not as smooth as the outbound flight (take off delays but that's par for the course in lisbon) but it was completely drama free, which makes this route a valid option for us to visit lisbon, in addition to easyjet from luton. :camera: top level of parque do alvito in monsanto, lisbon pxl20260529114928657.jpg pxl20260529133209262.jpg pxl20260529134332462.jpg

b: - nurseries were closed most afternoons this week, which meant that a good part of the working week was significantly disrupted. in any case, i started the weekend with the sense that it was a productive week. - "[...] so we're constantly pushing complex ideas through the eye of the needle of language.", the lossy compression of language. reading a light managerial book, completely disarmed, and suddenly i'm punched by something like this. - i finished the week with one of those still-elusive nights where i got to sleep for six hours almost in one go. the following day, we met friends at iwm duxford, an old wwii air base turned into a great air museum---one of my favourite places. since the last time we were there, they've built a nice playground with a very sensible layout (yes, i'm looking at you, bancroft gardens in hitchin). the children, of course, wanted to spend most of the day there. thankfully, it was built right next to the airstrip, so that we could keep an eye on the spitfires and hurricanes taking off and landing. we were disappointed, though, that we didn't get to see the corsair and the mustang pictured below fly. - i haven't watched any live formula 1 broadcasts this season yet. :camera: pxl20260628120449216.jpg

b: me, in portuguese: portugal, say por-tu-gal. 2-year-old a. in english: cro-co-dile! :smile: i spent some productive late evenings digital gardening. was i procrastinating, trying to put off an important task that needed to be done asap? no, not at all. as a result, the new features that i've been planning for some time have finally landed. here's a list of changes: - added autolinking the first occurrence of words or n-grams in markdown content to existing wiki node slugs, titles or aliases. it supports a blocklist file to specify nodes that are not meant to be autolinked. - added autolinking of words or n-grams to an external url, as mapped in a json file. - the weeknotes archive is now dynamically generated. - added better navigation to individual weeknotes. - applied typographical embellishments like auto replacing dashes with en- or em-dashes, straight quotes with curly quotes, and shortcodes with emojis. if something breaks, please let me know.

b: this saturday, we went to hertford to meet the lovely baby e for the first time. it's always nice to spend time in hertford—it's such a pleasant town. on the digital gardening front, i finished a new feature: the photos page, where all photos posted in weeknotes are scraped and displayed in a mosaic of thumbnails. there were also some fixes to the rss feeds to make them more standards-compliant. i have been trying to get back to trading some of my phone screen time for my kindle. since last year, i've been trying several ways of having a healthier relationship with my phone: uninstalling social apps, installing a more boring, text-based, application launcher, blocking loading certain websites in the browser, etc. besides using my phone more intentionally, i've been trying to increase the reading throughput of actual books as well. many people have adopted the ebook reader xteink x4, which, with its small form factor, fits comfortably in a pocket and can go anywhere. it's an interesting little device indeed. i may have large pockets but i think old 6" kindles are mostly pocketable too so it should do the job. :camera: sunflowers in bloom in our garden colourful and ornamented door in paddington cherry hinton hall park in cambridge cherry hinton hall park in cambridge by the river lea in hertford

b: - hi again - long time no see. - we've survived the challenging logistics of the summer school holidays (ssh)! i'm relieved to leave them behind. - we capped the ssh with another trip to lisbon. this was the one where we finally baptised our two daughters, after a few years of preparation and making sure we, family, godparents and witnesses were all in town at the same time. - i have, at some point, finished the screwtape letters and started sync by steven strogatz, which is fortunately a complete page-turner 20% in. more about the screwtape letters at another time, maybe. - this week my 2010 renault mégane has done its 100,000th mile. i've been thinking about replacing it with something newer for at least 3 years but i'm going to keep it, probably until the end. i asked myself why i would want a new car and couldn't come up with anything good. so, that's where my mind is right now. i was not the only owner but at least with me the car has been regularly serviced and it runs absolutely fine. - something else that happened this week was google's antigravity hackathon in their central saint giles office. as usual, google treats one of their important clients very well and it was nice to end a pleasant day winning the hackathon with the group i was in. - in the meantime, the static site generator underwent some deep refactors to correct some unfortunate design decisions that didn't prove useful in the end and to streamline publishing to github pages. what visibly changed was swapping the font from inter to ibm plex sans and there is now full-text search---see top right corner. :camera: the 2010 renault mégane turning 100,000 sunset with saturated colours
